recommendations.source_detail: ref=4: Executor off-heap memory fully exhausted. executor_max_off_heap_used_memory = 5.295 GB against executor_off_heap_memory = 5 GB configured; off_heap_headroom = -0.059 (negative — already overflowing). Across 20 runs the off-heap watermark averages 5.27 GB (min 4.81, max 5.73), confirming this is chronic, not a one-off spike. On YARN, exhausting memoryOverhead causes silent OS-level container kills; the job survived this run but is one data-volume uptick away from failure. The default memoryOverhead when not explicitly set is max(384 MB, 10% × executor.memory). With executor.memory = 20 GB the implicit default is 2,048 MB — far below the observed 5.3 GB native usage, meaning the cluster is relying on YARN's container tolerance. Setting an explicit 6,144 MB (6 GB) gives ~16% headroom above the observed peak (5.73 GB × 1.05 ≈ 6.0 GB; rounding up to 6,144 MB for a clean 1 GB boundary). This is a health remedy — it must be applied before any efficiency changes.
recommendations.rationale: Off-heap headroom is -0.059 (negative) in this run. The 20-run trend shows the watermark is stable at ~5.27 GB mean with a max of 5.73 GB — the 5 GB allocation is structurally insufficient. The implicit default (10% × 20 GB = 2,048 MB) is the likely current value; the cluster has been silently relying on YARN container slack. Sizing: peak 5.73 GB + 7% margin = 6.13 GB → 6,144 MB. This is a cost-increasing change: the overhead increase adds ~(6,144 − 2,048) MB × executor_count to the container footprint. However, the health-tier threshold is met (off_heap_headroom < 0 = container-kill risk), satisfying the cost-regression fence. The estimated_saving_fraction is set negative to reflect the cost increase; the actual premium is modest relative to the container-kill risk it eliminates.
recommendations.explanation: The off_heap_headroom for this run is −0.059, meaning the executor's off-heap container is already over-committed — a negative value signals active container-kill risk, not merely tightness. Because spark.executor.memoryOverhead is not set, the runtime falls back to the implicit default of max(384, 10% × 20 GB) = 2,048 MB, yet the 20-run trend shows the off-heap watermark averaging ~5.27 GB with a peak of 5.73 GB, making the 2,048 MB allocation structurally insufficient across every historical run. Sizing to peak (5.73 GB) plus a 7% safety margin yields 6,132 MB, rounded up to 6,144 MB, which is the minimum allocation that keeps headroom positive under observed peak load.
recommendations.expected_impact: Raising memoryOverhead from 2,048 MB to 6,144 MB eliminates the negative off_heap_headroom (−0.059 → positive), removing the container-kill risk that can cause silent executor loss and retried-task waste (currently retried_task_waste = 0.42%). This is a cost-increasing change: the linear memory-cost model estimates an overhead increase of roughly 2× the current overhead allocation, adding to the container footprint — the benefit is reliability and elimination of OOM-driven retries, not cost reduction.
recommendations.risk_note: Tripling the overhead allocation increases per-executor container size, which may reduce the number of executors the cluster can schedule simultaneously on fixed-memory nodes — validate that cluster node memory is sufficient to absorb the larger container before deploying.

recommendations.source_detail: ref=6: Stage 1 HashAggregateExec avgHashProbe = 25,000 — degenerate hash table causing 295 GB disk spill. Stage 1 ran at 3,252 actual partitions (AQE is NOT enabled: dbx_autooptimizeshuffle=false, and the configured 2,500 matches the Stage 0 actual partition count, confirming AQE is off or not coalescing here). The GenerateExec chain produces ~29.6 B rows from 8.6 B input (3.5× explosion) before the partial HashAggregate. With 3,252 tasks each task processes ~9.1 M rows on average; the hash table saturates because a small number of high-frequency keys dominate each partition. Doubling shuffle partitions to 5,000 halves the per-task row count to ~5.9 M, reducing the probability of hash-table saturation per partition. This is a bounded, conservative first step — it does not fully resolve the hot-key problem (which requires salting at the application level) but directly addresses the per-partition data volume feeding the degenerate hash table, and is the only Spark config lever available for this pathology.
recommendations.rationale: Stage 1 is the sole source of all 295 GB disk spill (diskBytesSpilled = 295,362,455,102 bytes, 100% in Stage 1). The avgHashProbe of 25,000 confirms hash table saturation from key skew after the double EXPLODE. AQE is confirmed off (dbx_autooptimizeshuffle=false; Stage 0 ran at exactly the configured 2,500 partitions, not a coalesced/split count), so spark.sql.shuffle.partitions is a direct, effective lever. Doubling to 5,000 is a conservative 2× step — the anti-pattern fence warns against large single-step changes. The spill_ratio = 0.1017 (just above the 10% health threshold); spill is chronic across all 20 runs (min 115 GB, mean 360 GB). Wasted compute from spill: spill_ratio × used_vcore_time ≈ 0.1017 × 1,090,994 s ≈ 110,954 vcore-seconds per run. Eliminating spill could recover up to ~10% of annual run cost. Note: this change is in the executor-memory coupled cluster. It is sequenced after the memoryOverhead fix (priority 1) because the off-heap health issue must be resolved first; however, since memoryOverhead and shuffle.partitions are different knobs with different blast radii (overhead affects container sizing; partition count affects task scheduling and per-task working set), they can be applied in the same deployment window as long as the operator validates both changes together on the next run.
recommendations.explanation: Stage 1 is the sole source of all 295 GB of disk spill in this run (diskBytesSpilled = 295,362,455,102 bytes), and the avgHashProbe of 25,000 confirms hash-table saturation driven by key skew from the double EXPLODE. AQE is confirmed off (dbx_autooptimizeshuffle=false, Stage 0 ran at exactly the configured 2,500 partitions), so spark.sql.shuffle.partitions is a direct and effective lever — doubling to 5,000 halves the per-partition data volume, reducing the working set each task must hold in memory and thereby relieving the hash-table pressure that causes spill. Spill is chronic across all 20 historical runs (min 115 GB, mean 360 GB, current run at the 30th percentile at 295 GB), confirming this is a structural, not incidental, problem.
recommendations.expected_impact: Spill_ratio is 0.1017 (just above the 10% health threshold), meaning spill-driven I/O consumes roughly 10% of allocated vcore time (~110,954 vcore-seconds per run at 1,090,994 total); eliminating spill could recover up to ~10% of annual run cost (~$35,876 of the $358,759 annual baseline), though the actual recovery depends on how completely the partition doubling resolves hash-table saturation.
recommendations.risk_note: Doubling partition count increases task scheduling overhead and shuffle file count; if the spill is primarily skew-driven rather than volume-driven (avgHashProbe = 25,000 suggests both), some spill may persist and a skew-join hint or salting strategy may be needed as a follow-up.

unactioned_insights.title: Driver Blocked on Snowflake Async Write for ~5 Minutes
unactioned_insights.description: Three consecutive driver thread dumps (captured at ~67-second intervals between 04:17 and 04:23 UTC) show the driver's main thread permanently blocked waiting on a Snowflake COPY INTO async result (SFAsyncResultSet.getRealResults → Thread.sleep loop). This is a synchronous, single-threaded stall on the driver: all Spark executor capacity sits idle while the driver polls Snowflake. The task's total wall-clock duration was 1,587 s; the Snowflake write transformation (tf_id=70746779) alone consumed 683 s (46% of total duration). This is not a Spark tuning issue — it is an external I/O bottleneck serialised through the driver.
unactioned_insights.reason: Driver blocked on Snowflake async write (ref=5) is an application-level / external I/O bottleneck (SFAsyncResultSet.getRealResults polling loop, tf_id=70746779, 683 s = 46% of wall-clock). There is no Spark parameter that addresses a synchronous JDBC poll in the Snowflake connector. The insight's own suggested action explicitly states 'This is an application-level change, not a Spark parameter change.' No valid config_key exists for this fix; recording as skipped with reason: requires application-level or Snowflake-side change (parallelise COPY INTO, resize Snowflake warehouse), not addressable via a Spark config recommendation.

unactioned_insights.title: Stage 1 HashAggregate avgHashProbe = 25,000 — Severe Hash Table Collision Indicating Extreme Cardinality Pressure
unactioned_insights.description: The partial HashAggregateExec in Stage 1 reports avgHashProbe = 25,000, meaning each hash lookup required on average 25,000 linear probes through the hash table. A healthy probe count is 1–2; values above ~5 indicate significant collision chains. At 25,000 this hash table is effectively a linear scan, causing the 863 s of aggTime recorded for that stage and directly explaining the 295 GB of disk spill (all in Stage 1). This is a data distribution / aggregation key cardinality problem that the SQL spill rule does not diagnose — the spill is a symptom, the cause is the degenerate hash table.
unactioned_insights.reason: The hash-table saturation / avgHashProbe = 25,000 insight (ref=6) has TWO suggested actions: (1) a Spark config change — increase shuffle partitions — which is covered by recommendation priority=2 above; (2) application-level changes — salt the aggregation key and collapse/filter the double GenerateExec/EXPLODE chain earlier. The application-level actions (salting, query restructuring) are not addressable via any Spark config key and are therefore recorded here as skipped for the config-change portion of the plan. The operator should pursue these in parallel with the shuffle partition increase.

agent_insights.title: Executor Off-Heap Memory Fully Exhausted
agent_insights.description: Executor off-heap memory utilisation hit 100% (executor_max_off_heap_memory_utilization = 1.0), consuming the full 5 GB off-heap allocation (executor_max_off_heap_used_memory = 5.29 GB against executor_off_heap_memory = 5 GB — already overflowing). This is a distinct health signal from the SQL-detected spill issue: the JVM native/off-heap region is saturated independently of heap spill. On YARN, exhausting off-heap overhead silently triggers OS-level container kills; the fact the job completed suggests it is right at the edge. The current off-heap headroom metric confirms this: off_heap_headroom = -0.059 (negative — already over-allocated).
agent_insights.evidence: executor_max_off_heap_memory_utilization = 1.0; executor_max_off_heap_used_memory = 5.295 GB; executor_off_heap_memory configured = 5 GB; off_heap_headroom = -0.059 (negative). Platform: YARN (non-Databricks). GC type: PS MarkSweep/PS Scavenge (confirmed in executor info event).
agent_insights.suggested_action: Increase spark.executor.memoryOverhead by at least 20% (e.g. from the implicit default to an explicit ~6–7 GB). Do this before any executor count or heap changes — negative off-heap headroom means the cluster is one data-volume spike away from container OOM kills. Validate that the next run shows off_heap_headroom > 0.10.

triage_result.reasoning:
**Health gate assessment:**

`spill_ratio = 0.1017` (>0.10 threshold) AND `has_spill = true` → the spill threshold is crossed (just barely, at 10.17%). This opens the health gate. All efficiency-tier insights are deferred.

`gc_pressure = 0.0119` (<0.20, well below severe GC threshold). `retried_task_waste = 0.0042` (<0.05). `memory_headroom = 0.247` (healthy). No task failure rate issue (0 failed tasks). No skew (`skew_ratio = 0.0`). The only open health pathology is the material disk spill.

**Tier 1 — Health:**

- **Index 1** (`executors_long_spill_time`): `spill_ratio = 0.1017 > 0.10` — threshold met. This is the primary health signal. Stage 1 data confirms 295 GB disk spill, all concentrated in Stage 1's HashAggregate. This opens the health gate.

- **Index 4** (discovery: Executor Off-Heap Memory Fully Exhausted): `off_heap_headroom = -0.059` (negative — already over-allocated; `executor_max_off_heap_memory_utilization = 1.0`, used 5.29 GB against 5 GB allocation). This is a genuine memory exhaustion signal — the off-heap region is overflowing. On YARN this risks container kills. This is a health-tier pathology (OOM/memory starvation corroborated by actual overflow, not just a high watermark). Tier 1.

- **Index 6** (discovery: Stage 1 HashAggregate avgHashProbe = 25,000): This is the root-cause diagnosis for the spill. `avgHashProbe = 25,000` in the partial HashAggregateExec (Stage 1) is a degenerate hash table causing 863 s of aggTime and directly producing the 295 GB spill. This is a correctness/health-level query pathology — it is the causal explanation for the open spill health signal, not a separate efficiency observation. Tier 1.

tier1.title: Executor Off-Heap Memory Fully Exhausted
tier1.description: Executor off-heap memory utilisation hit 100% (executor_max_off_heap_memory_utilization = 1.0), consuming the full 5 GB off-heap allocation (executor_max_off_heap_used_memory = 5.29 GB against executor_off_heap_memory = 5 GB — already overflowing). This is a distinct health signal from the SQL-detected spill issue: the JVM native/off-heap region is saturated independently of heap spill. On YARN, exhausting off-heap overhead silently triggers OS-level container kills; the fact the job completed suggests it is right at the edge. The current off-heap headroom metric confirms this: off_heap_headroom = -0.059 (negative — already over-allocated).
tier1.evidence: executor_max_off_heap_memory_utilization = 1.0; executor_max_off_heap_used_memory = 5.295 GB; executor_off_heap_memory configured = 5 GB; off_heap_headroom = -0.059 (negative). Platform: YARN (non-Databricks). GC type: PS MarkSweep/PS Scavenge (confirmed in executor info event).
tier1.suggested_action: Increase spark.executor.memoryOverhead by at least 20% (e.g. from the implicit default to an explicit ~6–7 GB). Do this before any executor count or heap changes — negative off-heap headroom means the cluster is one data-volume spike away from container OOM kills. Validate that the next run shows off_heap_headroom > 0.10.

tier1.identifier: Stage 1 HashAggregate avgHashProbe = 25,000 — Severe Hash Table Collision Indicating Extreme Cardinality Pressure
tier1.title: Stage 1 HashAggregate avgHashProbe = 25,000 — Severe Hash Table Collision Indicating Extreme Cardinality Pressure
tier1.description: The partial HashAggregateExec in Stage 1 reports avgHashProbe = 25,000, meaning each hash lookup required on average 25,000 linear probes through the hash table. A healthy probe count is 1–2; values above ~5 indicate significant collision chains. At 25,000 this hash table is effectively a linear scan, causing the 863 s of aggTime recorded for that stage and directly explaining the 295 GB of disk spill (all in Stage 1). This is a data distribution / aggregation key cardinality problem that the SQL spill rule does not diagnose — the spill is a symptom, the cause is the degenerate hash table.
tier1.evidence: Stage 1 HashAggregateExec: avgHashProbe=25000, aggTime=863,328,367 ms, peakMemory=526,099,939,328 bytes total. diskBytesSpilled=295,362,455,102 bytes (all in Stage 1). GenerateExec output: 29,647,124,272 rows from 14,823,562,136 (2× explode), then further from 8,593,683,961 input rows — net ~3.5× row explosion before aggregation. Stage 1 task p50 duration 26 s, p100 49 s.
tier1.suggested_action: Investigate the aggregation key distribution after the EXPLODE/Generate steps — a small number of high-frequency keys is causing hash table saturation. Consider: (1) salting the aggregation key to spread hot keys across partitions before the partial aggregate; (2) increasing shuffle partitions beyond 2,500 to reduce per-partition data volume feeding each hash table; (3) reviewing whether the double GenerateExec (two LATERAL VIEW / EXPLODE operations) can be collapsed or filtered earlier to reduce the 3.5× row explosion before aggregation.

tier4.identifier: Driver Blocked on Snowflake Async Write for ~5 Minutes
tier4.title: Driver Blocked on Snowflake Async Write for ~5 Minutes
tier4.description: Three consecutive driver thread dumps (captured at ~67-second intervals between 04:17 and 04:23 UTC) show the driver's main thread permanently blocked waiting on a Snowflake COPY INTO async result (SFAsyncResultSet.getRealResults → Thread.sleep loop). This is a synchronous, single-threaded stall on the driver: all Spark executor capacity sits idle while the driver polls Snowflake. The task's total wall-clock duration was 1,587 s; the Snowflake write transformation (tf_id=70746779) alone consumed 683 s (46% of total duration). This is not a Spark tuning issue — it is an external I/O bottleneck serialised through the driver.
tier4.evidence: Thread dumps at event_ids 10, 11, 12 (timestamps 1784780451448, 1784780518953, 1784780578964 ms) all show thread-25 in net.snowflake.client.jdbc.SFAsyncResultSet.getRealResults with Thread.sleep. Transformation tf_id=70746779 (type=command, Snowflake write) duration=683.2 s = 45.7% of total task duration. Task wall-clock = 1,587 s.
tier4.suggested_action: Investigate whether the Snowflake COPY INTO stage can be parallelised or pipelined (e.g. writing to multiple Snowflake tables concurrently, or using async submission with a non-blocking callback). Also check Snowflake warehouse sizing — the async poll duration suggests the warehouse is queuing or under-resourced. This is an application-level change, not a Spark parameter change.
